name: HashiCorp Vagrant
license: Business Source License 1.1 since Vagrant 2.4.0 (October 2023; source-available, not OSI open source); MIT before
summary: A command-line tool that builds the same development virtual machine for everyone from a `Vagrantfile` kept in the repo.
intro: You commit a `Vagrantfile` to the project: a short Ruby file, mostly plain assignments, naming a box (a packaged base image such as `bento/ubuntu-24.04`), the CPUs and memory, forwarded ports and provisioners. `vagrant up` downloads the box if it isn’t cached, asks a provider to create the machine, connects over SSH, mounts the project folder inside it at `/vagrant` as a synced folder, and on first boot runs the provisioners: shell scripts, Ansible, Chef, Puppet and others. VirtualBox, Hyper-V and Docker providers ship with Vagrant; VMware Fusion and Workstation need HashiCorp’s open-source plugin plus the VMware software, and libvirt/KVM a community plugin. Vagrant records which real machine belongs to the project in a `.vagrant` directory, so `vagrant ssh`, `halt` and `destroy` know what to act on, and one `Vagrantfile` can describe several machines, such as a web server and a database.

Vagrant is mature and changes slowly. It moved from the MIT licence to the Business Source License with 2.4.0 in October 2023; the latest stable release is 2.4.9 from August 2025, with only nightly builds since. HashiCorp is also shutting down HCP Vagrant, the hosted box catalog that replaced Vagrant Cloud: no new boxes since October 1, 2026, and the service closes on December 31, 2026, after which box owners must host box files themselves. For everyday app development, many teams now use a dev container instead: a container described by a `devcontainer.json` file, supported by VS Code, GitHub Codespaces and other tools. Vagrant still fits when you need a whole machine: a different operating system or kernel, Windows or BSD guests, or a multi-server setup to test provisioning scripts.
strengths: One command, `vagrant up`, gives every developer the same provisioned VM from a file in version control
Provisioning reuses real tools (shell, Ansible, Chef, Puppet), so the scripts that build production can be tested locally
Full virtual machines: other kernels, Windows or BSD guests, and multi-machine topologies that containers can’t imitate
Swap the provider (VirtualBox, Hyper-V, VMware, Docker, libvirt) without changing the workflow
limits: No longer OSI open source since 2.4.0; the BUSL blocks building a competing commercial product on it
HCP Vagrant, the public box catalog, closes on December 31, 2026; shorthand names like `bento/ubuntu-24.04` resolve against it, so teams need their own box hosting and `config.vm.box_url`
Slow release cadence: no stable release since 2.4.9 in August 2025
Full VMs are heavier and slower to start than containers; on Apple silicon, VirtualBox runs only Arm guests, so you need boxes built for arm64
The default synced folder doesn’t work on every host and guest combination; NFS, rsync and SMB synced folders are the alternatives, each with its own trade-offs

sections.title: Providers
sections.intro: A provider is what actually runs the machine. The `Vagrantfile` stays mostly the same; boxes are built per provider and, since 2.4.0, per CPU architecture.

rows.label: VirtualBox
values: The original and default provider. VirtualBox 7.1 added Arm Linux and BSD guests on Apple silicon Macs; Vagrant supports 7.1 from 2.4.2 and 7.2 from 2.4.9.

rows.label: Hyper-V
values: Windows 8.1 and later, with Hyper-V enabled.

rows.label: Docker
values: Runs the environment as containers; where Linux containers can’t run natively, Vagrant starts a host VM for Docker.

rows.label: VMware Fusion / Workstation
values: Official `vagrant-vmware-desktop` plugin plus the Vagrant VMware Utility
The plugin is open source (MPL); the VMware product is a separate install.

rows.label: libvirt (KVM, QEMU)
values: For Linux hosts; its last release was 0.12.2 in June 2023.

items.name: Vagrant
items.text: Pick it when the environment must be a real machine: a specific OS and kernel, Windows or BSD guests, several networked servers, or testing Ansible, Chef or Puppet code before it touches production.

items.name: Dev container
items.text: A `devcontainer.json` in the repo describes a container to code in. It is an open specification supported by VS Code, Visual Studio, IntelliJ IDEA, GitHub Codespaces and others, and suits most application work that runs on Linux.

items.name: Plain Docker Compose
items.text: If you only need the databases and queues an app depends on, a Compose file starts them as containers next to your normal editor, with no VM or dev environment at all.

story: Around 2010, web developers ran every project’s databases, queues and web servers on their own laptops, each at its own version, and teammates drifted apart: one on MySQL, another on PostgreSQL. In production, virtual machines on EC2 and similar clouds were already the norm. Vagrant’s early guide said it aimed to put “those very same principles” to work in development, with lightweight, reproducible virtual machines anyone on the team could rebuild.

Mitchell Hashimoto and John Bender started Vagrant on January 21, 2010, and released 0.1.0 on March 7 as a Ruby gem that drove Sun’s VirtualBox and provisioned machines with Chef or Puppet. It was a volunteer project, “not backed by any single company”. Vagrant 1.0 came out in March 2012, the year Hashimoto and Armon Dadgar founded HashiCorp, which went on to build Packer, Terraform and Vault alongside it.

Vagrant 1.1 in 2013 added providers, so the same workflow could drive VMware and other backends, and dropped RubyGems for installers that bundle Ruby. Vagrant 1.5 in 2014 launched Vagrant Cloud for sharing versioned boxes. In 2023 Vagrant moved to the Business Source License, and in 2026 HashiCorp began shutting down the hosted box registry, leaving the CLI as a self-hosted tool.

choices.choice: Configuration as a Ruby file in the repo
choices.why: One `Vagrantfile` per project, committed to version control, means every developer who clones the repo gets the same machine. The syntax is Ruby, but most files need little more than variable assignments, so users don’t have to know Ruby.
Vagrant “stands on the shoulders of giants”: VirtualBox ran the VM and Chef or Puppet set it up, so developers got environments built by the same scripts used for production.
Vagrant 1.1 separated the workflow from VirtualBox so the same commands could manage VMware, Hyper-V or Docker as well.

choices.choice: Installers instead of a Ruby gem
choices.why: Hashimoto found that most Vagrant users weren’t Ruby developers and many bugs came from broken Ruby setups, so from 1.1 Vagrant shipped as packages with Ruby and its libraries bundled.
